integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must state: (1) the improvement initially allows firms to earn supernormal profit (price £50 > new minimum ATC £40); (2) this triggers new entry; (3) entry increases market supply, driving price down below £50; (4) price falls to £40 (new long-run equilibrium where P = new minimum AC); (5) firms return to normal profit and produce at minimum AC (still 200 units, or unchanged quantity, since minimum occurs at same point); (6) productive efficiency is maintained because firms continue to produce at minimum AC in the new equilibrium. If answer fails to connect entry to price adjustment, or states price falls below £40, mark as incorrect.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Perfect competition achieves allocative efficiency because competitive firms are price-takers forced to produce where P = MC by market forces. Competition eliminates abnormal profit in the long run, driving firms to expand or contract until they produce at minimum AC. This dual outcome—P = MC and production at minimum AC—means perfect competition simultaneously satisfies allocative efficiency (price reflects true resource cost) and productive efficiency (no wasteful excess capacity). Without the P = MC condition that allocative efficiency defines, there would be no benchmark against which to assess whether competitive firms are truly allocating resources optimally; without allocative efficiency as the underlying principle, the competitive outcome would be just another quantity without normative meaning.

transferQuestion.questionText: A monopolist faces demand P = 50 − Q and has marginal cost MC = 10. It produces 20 units and charges a price of £30. Using allocative efficiency principles, explain why this monopoly outcome represents a welfare loss compared to what would occur under perfect competition, and calculate the allocative inefficiency in terms of the gap between what consumers value and what production costs.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify that: (1) under perfect competition, price would equal MC, so price would be £10 and quantity would be 40 units (solving 10 = 50 − Q); (2) the monopoly underproduces (20 vs 40 units) because it restricts output to raise price above MC; (3) for units 21–40, consumers' willingness to pay (given by demand curve) exceeds MC, meaning these units generate positive net benefit that is lost—allocative inefficiency occurs because P > MC at the monopoly quantity; (4) quantifying the loss requires identifying that each unit from 21 to 40 has marginal benefit (price on demand curve) minus MC, summing to deadweight loss. Accept numerical approximation of DWL area or clear identification that units 21–40 represent forgone welfare. Accept graphical description. Reject answers that mention only monopoly profit or that confuse allocative inefficiency with productive inefficiency.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a perfectly competitive industry, long-run equilibrium occurs at P = £8, Q = 1000 units market-wide, with each firm producing 10 units at minimum AC of £8. A regulator considers imposing a price ceiling of £6 to help consumers. Use allocative efficiency and the logic of perfect competition to explain (a) whether the price ceiling will improve or worsen allocative efficiency, and (b) what happens to firm entry/exit behaviour and why this matters for the sustainability of any efficiency gains.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must establish: (1) at P = £6, allocative efficiency breaks down because P < MC (since minimum AC = £8 > £6), meaning the firm cannot cover its full cost of production, so producing is allocatively inefficient—society wastes resources making units valued at £6 that cost £8 to produce; (2) firms cannot sustain production at P = £6 given their cost structure, triggering exit; (3) the price ceiling prevents the competitive mechanism (entry/exit) that normally maintains P = MC = minimum AC, so perfect competition cannot function—the market cannot remain in long-run equilibrium; (4) the conclusion must state that allocative efficiency worsens (P < MC is worse than P = MC) and the artificial price ceiling undermines the competitive process that achieves efficiency. Accept that allocative efficiency criterion directly implies this ceiling is inefficient. Reject answers that focus only on consumer surplus gains without addressing allocative efficiency definition (P vs MC) or that suggest entry will occur despite losses.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Productive efficiency is why perfect competition's long-run outcome matters. In short-run equilibrium, P=MC ensures allocative efficiency but firms may produce where AC is still falling or rising—wasting resources per unit. Only when firms are forced by competition to produce at minimum AC does productive efficiency emerge. Long-run entry and exit eliminate abnormal profit, leaving firms no choice but to operate at the lowest possible cost point. Without productive efficiency, allocative efficiency alone leaves the firm technically using the right quantity (P=MC) but doing so wastefully—the resources required per unit are higher than they need to be.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in a perfectly competitive market is in long-run equilibrium. Explain why P=MC alone does not guarantee that the firm is using resources without waste, and identify the additional condition required to ensure it is.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must state: (1) P=MC ensures the right output level is produced (allocative efficiency) but says nothing about the cost at which it is produced; (2) the firm must also produce at minimum AC (or the bottom of its AC curve) to be productively efficient—meaning resources are used in the least wasteful combination; (3) in long-run perfect competition, this is achieved because normal profit forces firms to operate at the AC minimum, so both conditions hold simultaneously. Accept alternative phrasing of 'minimum AC' such as 'lowest average cost per unit' or 'where MC cuts AC from below'. Incorrect if the answer conflates P=MC with productive efficiency or omits the need for output at minimum AC.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Two firms operate in different market structures. Firm X is in a perfectly competitive market in long-run equilibrium; Firm Y is a monopoly earning abnormal profit in the short run. Using the concepts of productive and allocative efficiency, explain why Firm X's situation differs from Firm Y's in terms of resource waste, and identify which firm is guaranteed to achieve productive efficiency.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) state that Firm X is forced to produce where P=MC=minimum AC due to normal profit in long-run equilibrium, achieving both allocative and productive efficiency; (2) explain that Firm Y, earning abnormal profit, has no pressure to move down its AC curve and may produce where AC is above its minimum, so resources per unit are wasted despite possible allocative efficiency failure (P>MC); (3) conclude that only Firm X is guaranteed productive efficiency because the exit threat eliminates abnormal profit and forces output at minimum AC, whereas Firm Y has no such constraint. Accept that Firm Y may produce at minimum AC by coincidence but is not guaranteed to. Incorrect if the answer claims Firm Y achieves productive efficiency or if it fails to link competitive pressure to the location of output on the AC curve.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Monopolistic competition's defining characteristic—that many firms coexist but each enjoys some pricing power through product differentiation—only remains stable because barriers to entry and exit are low. If barriers were high, differentiated firms could sustain supernormal profits indefinitely without new competitors entering to erode them, transforming the market into oligopoly or monopoly. Conversely, if exit barriers were high, struggling firms couldn't leave, forcing destructive price wars. Low barriers ensure the market self-corrects: excess profits attract new entrants, losses trigger exits, and this dynamic contestability keeps firms competing on both price and non-price factors rather than exploiting locked-in positions.

transferQuestion.questionText: A hairdressing market in a town has 15 established salons, each with loyal customers attracted by different styling reputations and price points. The local council suddenly introduces a licensing requirement and rental controls on salon premises that make it legally complex and financially prohibitive for new salons to open, though existing salons are grandfathered in. Using barriers to entry and exit, explain why this regulatory change would undermine the market's monopolistic competitive structure.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify that: (1) raising barriers to entry removes the contestability threat that previously disciplined existing firms' pricing and quality decisions; (2) without the threat of new entrants, the 15 salons can now sustain supernormal profits and reduce competitive pressure from non-price competition; (3) the market shifts away from monopolistic competition toward oligopoly characteristics because the many-firms-with-low-barriers condition is broken. Accept answers framed as 'firms no longer fear competition from new entrants' or 'the market becomes less contestable.' Reject answers that only describe the regulation itself without linking it to how barriers change competitive dynamics.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Two restaurants in a city close down each month on average, yet the market still contains 40 restaurants with differentiated menus and pricing. A rival city with identical demand has only 8 restaurants, none of which close annually. Explain which market is more likely to be monopolistically competitive, and use the concept of barriers to entry and exit to account for the difference in firm numbers.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) identify the first city as monopolistically competitive because the high exit rate and large firm count together indicate low barriers to exit and entry; (2) explain that low barriers allow unprofitable firms to exit quickly and new entrants to replace them, stabilising firm numbers at a higher equilibrium without requiring long-term survival of weak firms; (3) contrast the second city, where low exit rates and small firm count suggest high barriers preventing new entry or incumbent exit, so fewer firms can sustain themselves and dominant firms earn persistent supernormal profits (oligopoly or monopoly traits). Reject answers that attribute differences only to demand or cost differences without referencing how barriers to entry/exit shape the equilibrium number and churn of firms.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition, each firm's downward-sloping demand curve exists precisely because products are differentiated—if all firms sold identical goods, no individual firm could raise price without losing all customers to rivals. This differentiation is why the firm can apply the MC=MR rule to find its profit-maximising output: it has genuine price-setting power over its own product. Without product differentiation, there would be no individual demand curve to read the price from, and MC=MR would yield only a quantity, not a viable pricing decision. Differentiation is therefore the foundation that makes the short-run equilibrium model work.

transferQuestion.questionText: A coffee shop in a town centre operates in a monopolistically competitive market. It differentiates itself through speciality single-origin beans and a loyalty card scheme. The owner calculates that MC=MR occurs at 200 cups per day. At this output, the firm's demand curve shows a price of £3.50, and average total cost is £2.80. Explain why the coffee shop's ability to charge £3.50 (rather than being forced to charge the market price that all competitors charge) depends on its product differentiation strategy.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: The student must state that the downward-sloping demand curve—which allows the firm to charge £3.50 at 200 cups without losing all sales—exists only because the product is differentiated (speciality beans, loyalty scheme). Without differentiation, the firm would face a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve at a single market price; it could not choose to charge £3.50 independently. The differentiation creates the individual demand curve that the firm reads the price from after finding MC=MR output. Answers that merely restate the MC=MR rule or assume the firm has price-setting power without linking it to differentiation are incorrect.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Two firms in a monopolistically competitive industry both find that MC=MR at an output of 150 units. Firm A sells a generic product with minimal branding; Firm B has invested heavily in brand recognition and perceived quality differences. Using both the concept of product differentiation and the short-run equilibrium rule, explain why Firm B is likely to be able to charge a higher price than Firm A at the same MC=MR output quantity, and what this reveals about the role of differentiation in monopolistic competition.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: The student must explain that although both firms follow MC=MR to find output (150 units), they face different demand curves because of differentiation. Firm B's stronger brand and perceived quality create a steeper (less elastic) demand curve, so at 150 units, its demand curve intersects at a higher price point than Firm A's more elastic demand curve. This shows that differentiation does not just enable a firm to have a demand curve; the degree of differentiation determines the slope and position of that demand curve, which directly determines the price the firm can charge for any given output. Firm A's weak differentiation means its demand curve is nearly flat (close to perfect competition), whereas Firm B's strong differentiation gives it more price-setting power. Answers that discuss MC=MR without connecting it to how differentiation shapes the demand curve's elasticity, or that assume both firms charge the same price, are incorrect.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition, the firm's downward-sloping demand curve means price is not automatically set by the MC = MR rule—that rule only tells you the profit-maximising output quantity. Once you know output from MC = MR, you must use the demand curve to find what price customers will actually pay at that quantity. Without understanding MC = MR first, you would not know which output to read from the demand curve; without the demand curve, MC = MR alone cannot tell you the price. The two work sequentially: MC = MR determines output; demand curve determines price at that output.

transferQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm has identified that its MC = MR at an output of 150 units. At 150 units, its demand curve shows a price of £8 per unit. Its average total cost at 150 units is £6.50 per unit. Explain why the firm should produce 150 units and not 160 units, and state whether the firm earns supernormal profit at this short-run equilibrium.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: (1) The firm should produce 150 units because this is where MC = MR, meaning the revenue from the 150th unit equals its cost, so total profit is maximised. Producing 160 units would mean MC > MR (costs rise faster than revenue), reducing total profit. (2) The firm earns supernormal profit because at 150 units, AR (£8) > ATC (£6.50), so profit per unit is £1.50, giving total supernormal profit of £225. Any answer that correctly identifies MC = MR as the profit-maximising condition and correctly compares AR to ATC to determine profit type scores full marks. Incorrect: confusing the price (£8) with the MC = MR point; claiming the firm should produce where P = MC; failing to compare AR and ATC.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition discovers that at its current output of 120 units, MR = £3 and MC = £5. The demand curve shows price is £7 at 120 units, and ATC is £6. A rival firm enters the market with a very similar product. Predict what is likely to happen to the firm's demand curve and explain why the firm's short-run profit-maximising output will likely fall, using the MC = MR rule and the relationship between demand and price.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: (1) The new rival's similar product increases substitutes available, making the firm's demand curve more price elastic and shifts it leftward (demand falls). (2) With a leftward shift, the MR curve also shifts leftward/down. (3) At the current output of 120 units, MR is now below the (unchanged) MC of £5, so MC > MR, meaning the 120th unit costs more than it earns—total profit falls if this unit is produced. (4) The firm must reduce output back to where the new (lower) MR curve intersects the unchanged MC curve, restoring the MC = MR condition and maximizing profit at the new, lower level. (5) At the lower output, price is read from the new, leftward-shifted demand curve, likely lower than £7. Any response demonstrating that demand shift → MR shift → MC > MR at old output → output must fall to restore MC = MR scores full marks. Incorrect: claiming price falls before output adjusts; misunderstanding whether MR or MC shifts; failing to use MC = MR logic to explain the output change.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition, once a firm finds its profit-maximising output by setting MC=MR, it must determine what price to charge at that output. Since AR is the demand curve, the profit-maximising price is read directly from the AR curve at the MC=MR quantity—not read from the MC or MR curves themselves. This is essential: without knowing that AR equals the demand curve, a student might incorrectly try to read the price from the MR curve or fail to see that the firm's demand curve (AR) is the actual link between chosen output and feasible price. AR's identity as the demand curve ensures the price discovered this way is what customers will actually pay at that output level.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition has determined that MC=MR occurs at an output of 500 units. At this output level, its average revenue is £8 per unit and its average total cost is £7.50 per unit. Another firm in the same market finds MC=MR at 600 units, where its demand curve sits at £9 per unit and its ATC is £8.20. Which firm earns supernormal profit in the short-run equilibrium, and why?
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: The first firm earns supernormal profit (AR £8 > ATC £7.50). The second firm earns normal profit or loss (AR £9 is only relevant if we compare it to that firm's ATC £8.20, which gives £0.80 supernormal profit, but the comparison must use AR read from the demand curve at the MC=MR output). Accept: First firm clearly earns supernormal profit because AR (price from demand/AR curve at MC=MR output) exceeds ATC. Incorrect if: student confuses AR with MR, or fails to use the AR-as-demand-curve link to identify that £8 and £9 are the prices discoverable at those outputs.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm's demand curve is P = 20 − 0.5Q. Its total cost is TC = 50 + 4Q + 0.1Q². At the profit-maximising output, the firm charges a price of £12. Explain why the firm's actual profit or loss cannot be determined without first calculating its average total cost at the profit-maximising quantity, and identify what role the demand curve (AR curve) plays in establishing that profit-maximising price of £12.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct if answer includes: (1) Profit = TR − TC, and TR depends on P × Q; the price £12 comes from reading the AR/demand curve at the profit-maximising (MC=MR) quantity; (2) To find profit, ATC must be calculated and compared to AR (£12); if ATC < £12, supernormal profit; if ATC = £12, normal profit; if ATC > £12, loss; (3) The demand curve (AR) is the only source of the feasible price at any given output, so without it, the firm could not determine that £12 is the price it must charge at its chosen output. Incorrect if: student treats price as independent of demand curve, fails to explain why ATC comparison is necessary and sufficient, or confuses the role of MR (used to find quantity) with AR (used to find price).

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: The short-run MC=MR equilibrium in monopolistic competition may yield supernormal profit because differentiation and relatively inelastic AR initially allow price above average cost. However, this equilibrium is not final: the very existence of that supernormal profit triggers the entry/exit mechanism. New entrants shift incumbent demand curves leftward, eroding the gap between AR and AC that existed at the original MC=MR output. Understanding short-run equilibrium is essential because it identifies whether supernormal profit exists in the first place—without knowing firms are earning AR > AC at the MC=MR point, you cannot explain why entry happens or predict how the market structure evolves.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in a monopolistically competitive market is currently earning supernormal profit in the short run at output Q₁, where MC=MR. Explain why this short-run position will not persist, using the entry/exit mechanism.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify: (1) short-run supernormal profit signals attractive returns, prompting new entry; (2) new firms' products are substitutes, so entrants steal customers from existing firms; (3) incumbent firms' demand curves shift leftward; (4) this reduces AR relative to AC, eroding the supernormal profit that existed at the original MC=MR output. If the answer only describes entry without linking it to the supernormal profit revealed in short-run equilibrium, or mentions leftward demand shift without explaining why AR falls relative to AC, award partial credit only—the connection between the two concepts is not fully established.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a monopolistically competitive market, suppose a firm's short-run MC=MR equilibrium shows AR=£8 and AC=£6 at output 500 units. Entry of new firms causes the firm's demand curve to shift left; its new MC=MR equilibrium occurs at output 400 units with AR=£6.50 and AC=£6.20. Is the entry process complete, or will further adjustment occur? Justify your answer.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: further adjustment will occur. Justification must state that (1) at the new equilibrium AR (£6.50) still exceeds AC (£6.20), so supernormal profit (£0.30 per unit) still exists; (2) this continued supernormal profit signals further entry will occur; (3) the entry/exit mechanism is not complete until AR = AC. Answers that focus only on the size of profit or on entry itself, without explicitly connecting the persistence of AR > AC to the continuation of the entry mechanism, should not receive full credit.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Supernormal profit (AR > AC) is the trigger that sets the entry/exit mechanism in motion in monopolistic competition. New firms enter *because* they observe existing firms earning supernormal profit—that above-normal return signals profitable opportunity. Without supernormal profit existing first, there would be no incentive for entry; firms entering would have no reason to believe they could earn better returns than normal profit. The entry then mechanically reduces each incumbent's AR (via leftward demand shift), eroding the AR > AC gap that invited entry in the first place. The supernormal profit condition is therefore the prerequisite state that initiates the entire competitive process.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in a monopolistically competitive market currently has AR = £8 and AC = £5 at its profit-maximising output. Explain why this situation will not persist in the long run, and identify which of these changes is most likely to occur first: (i) the firm's demand curve shifts left, or (ii) new firms enter the market.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: (ii) new firms enter first. The AR > AC condition signals supernormal profit, which attracts new entrants (firms see profitable opportunity). Entry then causes the incumbent's demand curve to shift left. Acceptable explanation must identify that supernormal profit (AR > AC) is the signal that triggers entry, and that entry precedes the demand shift. Simply stating 'demand shifts' or 'profit falls' without linking it to the supernormal profit signal = incorrect.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a monopolistically competitive industry, firms initially earn AR = £12, AC = £9 at quantity 1,000 units each. Entry occurs, and each firm's demand curve shifts left; the new position is AR = £10, AC = £9.50 at quantity 900 units each. (a) Explain why entry has not yet restored long-run equilibrium. (b) What specific condition must be met for entry to stop?
integrationQuestion.markScheme: (a) Supernormal profit still exists: AR (£10) > AC (£9.50), so firms still earn above-normal returns. This will continue to attract further entrants. (b) Entry stops when AR = AC (normal profit only), meaning supernormal profit has been completely eroded. Both parts must be answered; part (a) must reference the AR > AC inequality to show understanding that supernormal profit persists; part (b) must state the AR = AC condition explicitly. Stating only 'profit falls' or 'firms have no incentive' without the AR/AC inequality = incomplete.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition only exists because entry and exit erodes supernormal profit. Without the mechanism of new firms entering when profits are high (and exiting when losses occur), firms would simply remain at whatever short-run position they reached. The tangency between demand and LRAC at normal profit is the *end state* of the entry/exit process, not a starting point. Entry/exit is the force that *drives* the demand curve leftward until tangency occurs. Understanding how competition erodes profit explains why equilibrium must involve normal profit and tangent curves—it answers the 'why does this position persist?' question.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in a monopolistically competitive market currently earns supernormal profit with AR > AC. Explain why this firm's demand curve will eventually shift leftward, and use this to explain why the firm cannot sustain supernormal profit in the long run.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) supernormal profit attracts new entrants into the market (low barriers); (2) new firms sell close substitutes, causing existing firm to lose some customers; (3) demand curve shifts left as a result; (4) this process continues until AR = AC (or demand is tangent to LRAC), at which point supernormal profit is eliminated and entry stops. Accept equivalent phrasing. Incorrect if student only describes tangency without explaining the entry mechanism that causes the demand shift, or if they state demand shifts without explaining why new entry causes this.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Suppose a firm in monopolistic competition experiences a sudden technological advance that reduces its average costs at all output levels. Explain why this firm will not remain at long-run equilibrium earning supernormal profit, even though its cost structure has improved.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) the technological advance creates a gap between AR and the new lower AC, generating supernormal profit; (2) supernormal profit signals market opportunity, attracting new entrants; (3) new firms' entry shifts this firm's demand curve leftward (and makes it more elastic); (4) leftward demand shift reduces the firm's price/quantity until AR falls back to the new AC level; (5) equilibrium is restored at normal profit, not supernormal profit. Accept that the firm's tangency point shifts downward and rightward due to lower costs, but the tangency still occurs at normal profit. Incorrect if student suggests the firm will keep supernormal profit because costs are lower, or if they omit the entry mechanism and its effect on demand.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Entry and exit in monopolistic competition work only because firms can distinguish between normal and supernormal profit. When new competitors enter and shift each firm's demand curve left, the existing firm's AR falls. Long-run equilibrium occurs precisely when AR has fallen enough to equal AC again—the tangency point. This equality is not an accident; it is the mathematical condition for zero supernormal profit. Without understanding that AR = AC means normal profit (not loss), you cannot explain why entry stops there, or why the firm has no incentive to leave even though it makes 'zero economic profit.' The firm *is* earning its opportunity cost reward; that is the point.

transferQuestion.questionText: In a monopolistically competitive market, a café initially sells 200 lattes per week at £3.50 each. Its long-run average cost is £2.80 per latte. After several new cafés open nearby, it now sells 160 lattes per week at £3.10 each. Assuming the café's long-run average cost remains £2.80, explain whether entry will continue or whether equilibrium has been reached. Use the relationship between AR and AC in your answer.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: Entry will continue. AR (£3.10) is still above AC (£2.80), so the firm earns supernormal profit of £0.30 per unit. This attracts more entrants, shifting demand further left. Equilibrium is reached only when AR falls to equal AC (£2.80), eliminating supernormal profit and the incentive for entry. Incorrect answer: Any response claiming equilibrium has been reached, or failing to compare AR to AC, or treating the profit per unit as 'zero' without reference to the normal profit built into AC.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A florist in monopolistic competition is currently in long-run equilibrium, with demand tangent to its long-run average cost curve at output Q. The florist's owner is offered a management job at another firm offering a salary £15,000 per year higher than her current implicit earnings. She leaves and sells the business. Using the relationship between AR, AC, and normal profit, explain why her exit does not violate long-run equilibrium theory in monopolistic competition, and what would have to change for her to stay.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: At tangency (long-run equilibrium), AR = AC, so the florist earns normal profit equal to the opportunity cost of her capital and entrepreneurship—built into AC. When offered a genuinely better outside opportunity (£15,000 more), her true opportunity cost rises, so normal profit as currently defined becomes insufficient. Long-run equilibrium is disrupted by the change in opportunity cost; she exits rationally. For her to stay, market conditions would need to shift so AR rises above the new, higher AC (reflecting her higher opportunity cost), restoring supernormal profit as an incentive to remain. Incorrect answer: Any response claiming equilibrium has been violated by her exit, or failing to recognize that the original AR = AC reflected her old opportunity cost, or suggesting she was making a loss in equilibrium.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: The diagram for monopolistic competition only makes sense once you understand that the firm is profit-maximising at MC=MR, not at the point where AR happens to equal AC. The visual trick is that in long-run equilibrium, AR and AC do touch (tangent), but that tangency is a *consequence* of the profit-maximising rule MC=MR, not the reason the firm stops there. Without grasping MC=MR, you cannot interpret why the demand curve shifts leftward in the long run—it shifts because supernormal profit (AR>AC at the short-run MC=MR output) attracts entrants—nor can you explain why the long-run equilibrium diagram shows tangency rather than an intersection.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition currently faces an AR curve and has MC=MR at an output of 500 units. At this output, AR=£8 and AC=£6. A new competitor enters the market. Explain why the firm's demand curve must shift, and sketch or describe where the new long-run equilibrium position will be found on the diagram. Explain how you would identify this position using the profit-maximising rule.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) The firm currently earns supernormal profit (AR £8 > AC £6), attracting new entrants. (2) New entrants' entry causes the firm's demand (AR) curve to shift left and/or become more elastic because market share falls and substitutes increase. (3) Long-run equilibrium occurs where MC=MR at the new lower output level, and at this point AR=AC (tangency), eliminating supernormal profit. (4) The firm identifies this position by locating MC=MR first, then reading AR off the demand curve, which now touches AC at that output. Answers that identify tangency as the starting point for finding equilibrium, rather than as a consequence of MC=MR, are incorrect.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a monopolistically competitive market, one firm's short-run equilibrium shows AR=£12, AC=£10, and MC=MR at 400 units. A rival firm enters and the first firm's demand shifts. Eventually, the first firm reaches a long-run equilibrium where MC=MR at 320 units, and AR=£9. Without calculating, explain whether this firm's AC at 320 units must be £9 or could be different, and justify your answer using both the profit-maximising rule and the condition for long-run equilibrium.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: AC at 320 units must be £9. Justification must state: In long-run equilibrium, the firm still profit-maximises at MC=MR (the output rule is unchanged). At long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition, there is zero supernormal profit, meaning AR=AC at the profit-maximising output. Since AR=£9 at the MC=MR output of 320 units, AC must equal £9 at that same output (tangency condition). Any answer stating AC could be different, or that tangency alone determines equilibrium without reference to MC=MR, is incorrect.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: The tangency condition in long-run monopolistic competition equilibrium is not arbitrary—it is the graphical consequence of the entry process itself. As new firms enter, each incumbent firm's demand curve shifts leftward. Entry stops only when the leftward-shifting demand curve can no longer lie above the AC curve at the profit-maximising point (MC=MR). This occurs precisely when AR becomes tangent to AC: any further entry would push demand below AC everywhere, making losses inevitable. The tangency is therefore the equilibrium state where entry pressure ceases because supernormal profit has been eliminated. Without understanding that tangency represents the endpoint of competitive entry eroding profit, the diagram becomes just a geometric coincidence rather than an explanation of why firms cease earning supernormal profit in long-run equilibrium.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition earns supernormal profit in the short run. Explain, using a diagram, why the firm's demand curve must shift and why the long-run equilibrium position occurs where this new demand curve becomes tangent to the AC curve, rather than at some point where demand still lies above AC.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify: (1) entry of new competitors in response to supernormal profit; (2) each incumbent firm's demand shifts left as the market expands/rivals take market share; (3) at tangency, AR=AC, eliminating supernormal profit and removing the incentive for further entry; (4) if demand remained above AC at MC=MR, supernormal profit would persist and entry would continue, so tangency is the stopping point. Diagram should show initial short-run AR above AC at MC=MR, and new long-run AR tangent to AC at a lower output. Award mark if student correctly explains why tangency (not some other position with AR>AC) represents equilibrium.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm's long-run equilibrium is at an output of 500 units where AR=AC=£8. A new production technology reduces AC uniformly by £1 per unit. Explain why, in the subsequent long-run equilibrium after other firms adopt this technology, the firm will once again produce an output where AR is tangent to its new AC curve, and why output will be lower than 500 units despite the fall in costs.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify: (1) the fall in AC creates supernormal profit (AR>AC) at the original output; (2) this attracts new entrants, shifting each firm's demand curve left; (3) entry continues until the new, lower AC curve is tangent to the now-lower demand curve; (4) although AC has fallen, demand shifts left by enough that the tangency point lies at lower output, because the lower cost attracts enough entry to more than offset the cost saving. Award mark if student explains that tangency is restored (not that profit disappears at some other point) and correctly reasons that lower demand at tangency can coincide with lower AC yet lower output.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: The MC curve is essential for locating the profit-maximising output in monopolistic competition. Since the firm chooses output where MC = MR (the decision rule), you must know where MC intersects MR on the diagram to find the quantity to produce. Without MC, you cannot identify this intersection point, so you cannot determine the profit-maximising quantity or read off the price from the AR curve. In long-run equilibrium, MC = MR must hold at the point where AR is tangent to AC; if MC were absent or misplaced, you could not verify that this tangency represents true profit-maximisation rather than just cost minimisation.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition has MR and AR curves already drawn on a diagram. The firm's cost structure shows MC initially falls from £8 to £4 over the first 10 units of output, then rises to £6 at 15 units and £9 at 20 units. The MR curve intersects the horizontal line at £7. At what output level does the firm maximise profit, and why is the shape of the MC curve (not just its existence) relevant to your answer?
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: 15 units. The firm maximises profit where MC = MR; since MR = £7, the student must identify that MC = £7 occurs at 15 units of output (because MC has risen from £6 at 15 units—this is the only intersection). The shape matters: if MC were flat or falling, there would be no intersection at £7, or a different one. The U-shape ensures MC rises to meet the falling MR, creating a single clear profit-maximising point. Incorrect if student picks 10 units (confusing minimum MC with MC = MR), picks 20 units, or fails to justify why the rising portion of MC is necessary.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In long-run monopolistic competition equilibrium, a firm's AR curve is tangent to its AC curve, and both MC and MR pass through the tangency point. Explain why the MC curve must be rising (not falling or flat) at this equilibrium output for the tangency to represent a genuine profit-maximising outcome, and not a profit-minimising one.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must establish: (1) At the tangency, MC = MR by the profit-maximisation rule. (2) If MC were falling at this point, then for a small increase in output, MC would fall below MR, making it profitable to expand further—contradicting equilibrium. (3) If MC were flat or falling, the firm would not actually be maximising profit at the tangency; it would want to move along MR. (4) MC must be rising so that any movement away from the tangency output (either side) causes MC to diverge from MR in a way that reduces profit, confirming the tangency is a maximum, not a minimum. Accept answers that clearly show MC rising ensures the second-order condition for profit maximisation at the tangency point. Incorrect if student ignores the shape of MC, states only that MC = MR without addressing why rising MC is necessary, or confuses this with long-run entry/exit dynamics.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition diagrams, the AC curve is essential for identifying whether a firm earns supernormal or normal profit. The vertical distance between the AR curve and AC curve at the profit-maximising output (MC=MR) determines the profit rectangle. Without understanding AC's U-shape and how it shifts with scale, you cannot correctly locate the tangency point in long-run equilibrium where AR becomes tangent to AC. The shape of AC also explains why the tangency occurs *before* minimum efficient scale: if AC were still falling, AR couldn't be tangent to it—MC would still lie below AC. The AC curve's geometry thus constrains where long-run equilibrium must lie.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition has a short-run average cost curve that reaches its minimum of £8 per unit at 500 units of output. The firm's demand curve intersects its marginal cost curve (where MC=MR) at 400 units, where the price is £10 per unit. Explain whether this firm is earning supernormal or normal profit in the short run, and identify which point on the AC curve is relevant to your answer.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct: The firm earns supernormal profit. At 400 units, AR (£10) exceeds AC (which must be above its minimum of £8 because 400 < 500, the minimum point). The relevant AC is the point on the AC curve corresponding to 400 units of output, not the minimum AC. The profit rectangle is drawn between AR and this AC value. Incorrect: any answer stating normal profit, or identifying only the minimum AC point as relevant, or confusing where MC=MR occurs with where AC is minimised.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition, a firm's demand curve is tangent to its average cost curve at 600 units of output, where both equal £12. Explain why the firm cannot be producing at the minimum point of its AC curve, and use the relationship between AC and MC to justify why tangency (not intersection) must occur at equilibrium.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct: At tangency, AR=AC (£12) and MC=MR (the profit-maximising condition). If the AC curve were still at its minimum point, MC would equal AC, so MR would also equal AC. But then AR > MR (demand always lies above MR in monopolistic competition), creating a contradiction: AR cannot simultaneously equal AC and exceed MR=AC. Therefore tangency must occur where AC is still falling (or just past its minimum but rising slowly), where MC < AC initially, allowing the downward-sloping AR and upward-sloping MC to meet MR while AR remains tangent to AC. Incorrect: answers that state the minimum AC point is reached, or that confuse tangency with intersection, or that do not explain the logical impossibility using the AC/MC relationship.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition diagrams, the downward-sloping demand curve you draw IS the AR curve. This matters because it fixes where you read the price: at the profit-maximising output (where MC=MR), you must go vertically up from that quantity to the AR curve, not to MR. The vertical distance between AR and AC at that output shows supernormal profit or loss. Without recognising that AR is the demand curve, you cannot correctly identify the price charged, locate supernormal profit geometrically, or understand why the long-run adjustment involves the demand curve shifting left—it shifts because AR (the demand each firm faces) contracts as new competitors enter.

transferQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm has the following short-run position: at its profit-maximising output of 400 units, MR = MC = £8, AC = £10, and its demand curve shows a price of £12. Calculate total supernormal profit and explain why the price cannot be read from the MR curve instead of the demand curve.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: Total supernormal profit = (£12 – £10) × 400 = £800. Explanation must state: the price charged is £12 (from the demand/AR curve at 400 units), not from MR; MR shows the additional revenue from the last unit sold, not the price per unit; only AR (the demand curve) tells us the price at which quantity is sold. Reading price from MR would be incorrect because MR lies below AR and does not represent the price per unit. Award mark only if both the numerical calculation and the conceptual explanation of why AR (not MR) determines price are correct.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm's demand curve shifts leftward from D₁ to D₂ in the long run due to new entrants. The firm's AC curve is U-shaped with minimum at £6. On the original demand curve D₁, at the profit-maximising output, the firm's supernormal profit was £2 per unit. Using the concept that AR = demand curve, explain what must be true about the position of D₂ relative to the AC curve, and why the firm's supernormal profit becomes zero even though AC has not changed.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must state: D₂ (the new AR curve) must be tangent to the AC curve at the new profit-maximising output where MC = MR₂. Explanation must include: as demand shifts left, AR also shifts left; the firm's AR is lower at every output level, so even though MC = MR at the new output, AR can now equal AC because the AR curve has moved down/left to meet AC; supernormal profit becomes zero (AR = AC) not because costs fell, but because the demand (AR) the firm faces has contracted, lowering the price it can charge at its chosen output. Award mark only if both the geometric relationship (tangency of D₂ to AC) and the causal logic (AR shift, not AC change, eliminates profit) are clearly stated.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition, the demand curve's elasticity directly determines where MR sits relative to AR, which then governs whether supernormal profit exists in the short run. Because firms face downward-sloping demand (some market power from differentiation), MR must lie below AR and fall steeply. This gap between MR and AR is crucial: the firm's profit-maximising decision (MC=MR) yields an output where price (read from AR) exceeds marginal cost, but the size of that markup—and thus whether AR can also exceed AC to create supernormal profit—depends entirely on how far MR has dropped below AR at that quantity. Without understanding MR's geometric relationship to the downward-sloping demand curve, you cannot correctly position the profit rectangle or recognise why long-run entry erodes it.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition has demand P = 50 − 2Q, and therefore MR = 50 − 4Q. At the profit-maximising output where MC = MR, suppose MC = 30 and the firm's average cost is AC = 35. Is the firm earning supernormal profit, normal profit, or making a loss in the short run? Show your working.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct: The firm is earning supernormal profit. Working: MC = MR means 30 = 50 − 4Q, so Q = 5. Price (from AR/demand) = 50 − 2(5) = 40. Since AR (=40) > AC (=35), supernormal profit is earned. Incorrect: Any other answer, including stating normal profit or a loss, or failing to distinguish between MC=MR output and the price read from the demand curve.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In the short run, a monopolistically competitive firm maximises profit where MC = MR at output Q1, earning supernormal profit because AR > AC. Explain why, as new firms enter the industry in the long run, the firm's MR curve shifts, and why this process must continue until the MR curve intersects the new (leftward-shifted) demand curve at exactly the point where AR is tangent to AC.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) Entry of new firms reduces this firm's market share, shifting its demand curve left and making it more elastic; (2) The new demand curve is steeper (more elastic), so MR also lies below it but is less steep than before; (3) At the original Q1, AR now falls below AC, eliminating supernormal profit and making entry unprofitable; (4) Exit/contraction occurs until a new equilibrium where the flatter demand curve's MR intersects at a point where that demand curve is tangent to the (unchanged) AC curve, guaranteeing AR = AC at the MC = MR output, leaving only normal profit. Incorrect: Any answer omitting the link between demand elasticity change and MR repositioning, or failing to explain why tangency specifically ensures the profit-maximising output also yields zero supernormal profit.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition is necessary to understand why the market remains inefficient. Because entry continues until supernormal profit is eliminated—forcing tangency of AR to ATC on the downward-sloping section—the equilibrium output is necessarily below minimum ATC. Without understanding that normal profit pins the firm at this tangency point, you cannot explain why monopolistic competitors cannot reach the lowest-cost output level that perfect competitors achieve. The tangency itself is the structural reason for both productive and allocative inefficiency.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in a monopolistically competitive market currently earns supernormal profit. Explain why the resulting long-run equilibrium will be productively inefficient, using the concept of entry and the position of the demand curve relative to ATC.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) new firms enter because of supernormal profit; (2) entry shifts the firm's AR curve left; (3) AR becomes tangent to ATC, eliminating supernormal profit; (4) tangency occurs on the downward-sloping part of ATC, not at its minimum; (5) therefore output is less than the output that minimizes ATC = productive inefficiency. Any answer that merely states 'firms make normal profit' without linking entry, leftward shift, and tangency position to the ATC curve receives no credit.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A monopolistically competitive firm's long-run equilibrium is at output 500 units, where AR = ATC = £12 and MC = £8. Using this information and your understanding of entry, explain (a) why this firm is allocatively inefficient, and (b) why a perfectly competitive firm in long-run equilibrium could not have these same values.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (a) Price (£12, from AR) exceeds MC (£8), so allocative inefficiency exists because marginal benefit to society exceeds marginal cost; this arises because AR is downward-sloping, which would not occur after entry in perfect competition. (b) In perfect competition, long-run equilibrium requires entry to continue until AR = ATC = MC at minimum ATC; here MC < ATC, so either entry would still be occurring (not equilibrium) or ATC is not at its minimum (contradicting perfect competition's result). Any answer that does not explicitly connect the downward-sloping AR to the allocative inefficiency or does not reference the minimum ATC requirement in perfect competition receives no credit.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Monopolistic competitors fail allocative efficiency because their downward-sloping demand curves force price above marginal cost at long-run equilibrium. Since P > MC, consumers value additional units more than the resources required to produce them—yet firms don't expand output. This violates the P = MC condition for allocative efficiency. The gap between price and MC measures the allocative loss: society would gain welfare if output increased, but product differentiation and low barriers to entry prevent it. Unlike perfect competitors (where P = MC at equilibrium), monopolistically competitive firms cannot eliminate this allocative inefficiency even in long run, making it a structural feature of their market, not a disequilibrium problem.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition has marginal cost of £8 per unit and faces a demand curve where the long-run equilibrium price is £12 per unit. Using the concept of allocative efficiency, explain why this firm's output is allocatively inefficient and what this tells us about the relationship between consumer valuation and resource cost.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) identify that P (£12) > MC (£8), and (2) explain that this means consumers value extra units (£12) more than the resources used to produce them cost (£8), so welfare would increase by producing more output. Award mark only if both elements are present. Incorrect if student states the firm should produce where P = MC without explaining why the gap matters for consumer vs. resource valuation, or if numerical comparison is reversed.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Compared to a perfectly competitive industry in long-run equilibrium, a monopolistically competitive industry with identical cost structures produces lower total output and charges a higher price. Using allocative efficiency and the long-run equilibrium conditions of monopolistic competition, explain why this price–output outcome necessarily follows from product differentiation, and what efficiency loss results.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must demonstrate: (1) in perfect competition, P = MC at long-run equilibrium; (2) in monopolistic competition, P > MC because the downward-sloping demand curve created by product differentiation means AR lies above MC at the MC = MR point; (3) since P > MC in monopolistic competition but P = MC in perfect competition, the monopolistically competitive industry produces where the gap between consumer valuation (P) and marginal resource cost (MC) is positive, creating allocative deadweight loss (or stating that fewer mutually beneficial transactions occur). Award mark only if logical chain connecting differentiation → downward-sloping demand → P > MC → allocative inefficiency is explicit. Incorrect if allocative efficiency concept is not applied to explain the comparison.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: In monopolistic competition, firms cannot achieve productive efficiency because their downward-sloping demand curves force them into long-run equilibrium where AR=ATC on ATC's falling section—not at ATC's minimum. Productive efficiency requires producing where AC is lowest (where MC cuts AC from below), but the firm's lower-sloping demand constraint prevents this. The tangency point comes before minimum AC is reached, leaving unused capacity. This divergence from perfect competition is why monopolistic competitors must accept higher per-unit costs as the price of product differentiation.

transferQuestion.questionText: A firm in monopolistic competition reaches long-run equilibrium producing 80 units weekly. Its ATC at 80 units is £12, and minimum possible ATC (at its lowest point) is £10 when producing 120 units. Using the concept of productive efficiency, explain why this firm is operating with excess capacity and cannot move to the 120-unit output.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify that: (1) productive efficiency requires output at minimum ATC (120 units, £10); (2) the firm's downward-sloping demand curve forces equilibrium where AR=ATC at only 80 units; (3) the firm cannot expand to 120 units because MR would fall below MC at that higher output, violating the profit-maximising condition MC=MR required in monopolistic competition equilibrium. Accept: 'the demand constraint prevents access to the minimum AC point' or 'moving to 120 units would make MR<MC, destroying equilibrium.' Reject answers that only describe the inefficiency without explaining why the demand-curve slope prevents productive efficiency.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Two firms both produce at output levels where ATC=£15 in long-run equilibrium. Firm X (perfect competition) operates at the minimum point of its ATC curve; Firm Y (monopolistic competition) operates on the downward-sloping section of its ATC curve. Using your understanding of productive efficiency and the difference between horizontal and downward-sloping demand curves, explain why Firm Y's demand curve makes productive efficiency impossible to achieve, whereas Firm X's does not.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must establish: (1) Firm X has a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve, so AR=Price is constant; at MC=MR equilibrium, MR equals this constant price, and this occurs exactly where MC cuts the minimum point of ATC, achieving productive efficiency; (2) Firm Y has a downward-sloping demand curve, so AR falls as output rises; this means MR<AR and falls faster than AR; when MC=MR equilibrium is reached, the corresponding point on AR (demand curve) is higher up, on the falling section of ATC, before minimum ATC; (3) therefore Firm Y cannot produce at minimum ATC without breaking MC=MR equilibrium. Accept: 'horizontal demand allows equilibrium at minimum AC; downward slope forces equilibrium before minimum AC is reached.' Reject: answers that only contrast productive and allocative efficiency without linking to the demand-curve slope.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Barriers to entry and exit are not unique to oligopoly, but oligopolies depend on them to survive as concentrated markets. Without high barriers, the few firms in an oligopoly would face constant threat of new entrants eroding their market share and profit margins, turning the market contestable. The high barriers in oligopoly specifically prevent this contestation: they lock in existing firms' dominance and lock out rivals. Without understanding barriers as the mechanism that *protects* market concentration, you cannot explain why oligopolies remain oligopolies rather than fragmenting into perfect competition.

transferQuestion.questionText: A telecommunications market is dominated by three large firms with established networks and brand recognition. A new firm wishes to enter but faces £2 billion in infrastructure costs that cannot be recovered if it exits. Explain why this barrier to entry is particularly significant for maintaining oligopolistic market structure in this case.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify that the high sunk cost creates a barrier to entry that protects the three existing firms' market share by discouraging new competitors from joining, thereby maintaining the concentration of the market in few hands rather than allowing it to become contestable. Incorrect: merely describing the sunk cost without linking it to market protection or contestability; or claiming the barrier makes oligopoly inevitable without explaining the protective mechanism.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A firm in an oligopolistic market is considering leaving the industry because profits have fallen. However, it is locked into a 10-year supply contract and owns highly specialised manufacturing equipment worth £50 million that has no alternative use. Using both the concept of barriers and the structure of oligopoly, explain why this firm may be forced to remain in the market despite losses, and what this reveals about oligopolistic stability.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) identify that sunk costs and contractual obligations form barriers to exit, making it costly to leave; (2) recognise that these same barriers that protect incumbents from new entry also trap existing firms in the market; (3) conclude that this explains why oligopolistic concentration persists even when individual firms are unprofitable—the barriers work both ways to lock in market structure. Incorrect: discussing exit costs without linking to market structure maintenance; or treating entry and exit barriers as separate unrelated phenomena; or failing to connect barriers to oligopoly's structural persistence.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: A high concentration ratio (oligopoly characteristic) is the *outcome* that n-firm concentration ratio *calculation* measures. You need to know how to calculate n-firm ratios precisely because the resulting percentage is what tells you whether an oligopoly actually exists. Without performing the calculation—summing the top firms' market shares—you cannot determine whether market concentration is high enough to constitute oligopoly, or whether the market is competitive instead. The calculation converts raw firm size data into the single number that defines the oligopoly threshold.

transferQuestion.questionText: In a market, five firms have annual sales of £120m, £85m, £60m, £45m, and £30m respectively. Remaining firms share £160m in sales. Calculate the five-firm concentration ratio and explain whether this market shows the high concentration characteristic of oligopoly.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: CR5 = 85% (340m ÷ 500m × 100). Explanation must state that 85% is high enough to indicate oligopoly because a small number of firms (five) supply the vast majority of output, leaving many smaller competitors with minimal market share, meeting the oligopoly definition. Accept equivalent wording. Incorrect calculation or failure to link the 85% result to oligopoly characteristics = no mark.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Firm A operates in Industry X where the three-firm concentration ratio is 72%, and in Industry Y where it is 34%. In which industry is Firm A more likely to experience a significant effect on market price from its own output decisions? Use concentration ratio calculations to justify your answer.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: Industry X. Justification must recognise that the 72% CR3 means the three largest firms (including A) supply most of the market, so any one firm's output change alters total market supply noticeably, affecting price. By contrast, 34% CR3 means many firms share the market, so A's output decisions have negligible market effect. Accept answers that reason from the oligopoly characteristic (few firms, high interdependence) directly enabled by high concentration ratio measurement.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Concentration ratios only have meaning if you can calculate them accurately first. The numerical result—whether it's 45% or 78%—is what signals whether a market is oligopolistic or competitive. Without precise calculation of each firm's market share and correct summation of the top n firms, you cannot distinguish a genuinely concentrated market from a fragmented one. The significance of a concentration ratio (its use in assessing market power and regulatory concern) depends entirely on trusting the arithmetic: a miscalculated CR5 would misdirect policy and misjudge competitive pressure.

transferQuestion.questionText: A market has four firms with annual revenues of £240m, £160m, £120m, £80m, and all other firms combined accounting for £400m. Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio (CR4) and explain whether this result would typically concern a regulator investigating oligopolistic behaviour.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct CR4 = 60% (firm shares: 30%, 20%, 15%, 10%; sum of top 4 = 75% is INCORRECT; recalculate: total industry = £1,000m; top 4 firms = £600m; CR4 = 60%). At 60%, this is at or above the threshold typically associated with oligopoly, so regulators would likely view it as concerning and warrant investigation into market power and potential anti-competitive conduct. Answer must show correct calculation AND link the 60% figure to regulatory significance (oligopoly concern). Partial calculations without the link to significance do not merit full credit.

integrationQuestion.questionText: The five-firm concentration ratio in an industry is 65%. A merger between the third and fourth largest firms would increase their combined market share from 18% to 22%. Using your understanding of both how concentration ratios are calculated and why they matter, explain why a competition regulator might block this merger, and how the CR5 would change after the merger.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Student must: (1) recognise that the CR5 would rise from 65% to 69% (add the 4% increase to the existing CR5), demonstrating understanding that the calculation sums the top 5 firms' shares and a merger consolidates shares upward; (2) explain that moving from 65% to 69% deepens oligopolistic concentration, reducing the number of independent competitors and increasing the merged firms' collective influence over price and output; (3) conclude that regulators block such mergers precisely because the resulting concentration ratio signals diminished competition and increased consumer harm risk. Answer must integrate the mechanical calculation (how CR5 changes) with the economic significance (why this change matters for market power).

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: A payoff matrix is essential for identifying a dominant strategy because you must compare a firm's payoffs across all possible rival actions to determine if one strategy always yields the highest return. Without the matrix's systematic layout of every strategy combination and its corresponding payoffs, you cannot verify whether a strategy truly dominates all alternatives regardless of what the rival does. The matrix structure makes the comparison visible and exhaustive; it transforms the abstract question 'which strategy is best no matter what?' into a concrete check across every row or column.

transferQuestion.questionText: Two firms, Alpha and Beta, are deciding whether to invest heavily in R&D or invest minimally. The payoff matrix (Alpha's profit, Beta's profit in £m) is: Heavy R&D / Heavy R&D (8, 8); Heavy R&D / Minimal (5, 12); Minimal / Heavy R&D (12, 5); Minimal / Minimal (9, 9). Does Alpha have a dominant strategy? Justify your answer using the payoff matrix.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct: No, Alpha does not have a dominant strategy. To justify: when Beta chooses Heavy R&D, Alpha earns 8 from Heavy R&D and 12 from Minimal (so Minimal is better). When Beta chooses Minimal, Alpha earns 5 from Heavy R&D and 9 from Minimal (so Minimal is better). Minimal appears best against both rival choices, making it a dominant strategy for Alpha. (Incorrect: claiming Alpha has Heavy R&D or no strategy without checking both columns; or claiming Minimal is dominant without comparing payoffs across both of Beta's possible moves.)

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a modified payoff matrix, Firm X discovers it has a dominant strategy (Strategy P) over Strategy Q. However, Firm X also observes that if both firms mutually adopt their dominant strategies, the combined industry profit is lower than if both chose their non-dominant strategies. Explain why this situation can occur and identify what this outcome reveals about the structure of the payoff matrix.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) A dominant strategy maximises one firm's individual payoff regardless of the rival's choice, not industry profit—these are different objectives. (2) The payoff matrix reveals a conflict between individual rationality (each firm choosing its dominant strategy) and collective rationality (joint profit maximisation). (3) This illustrates the Prisoners' Dilemma game structure, where dominant strategies lead to a mutually worse outcome than cooperation would. (4) The payoff matrix's structure shows that mutual defection (both choosing dominant strategies) yields lower payoffs in the 'both cooperate' cell than in the 'both defect' cell, but higher payoffs for each individual defector if the rival cooperates. Incorrect: only describing what a dominant strategy is without explaining the divergence between individual and joint incentives; or claiming the payoff matrix is faulty rather than recognising the conflict it reveals.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: A dominant strategy guarantees a firm's best payoff regardless of rivals' moves; a Nash equilibrium occurs when each firm's chosen strategy is optimal given what rivals have chosen. If a firm has a dominant strategy, it will always play it—so a Nash equilibrium must include that dominant strategy for that firm. Conversely, Nash equilibrium may exist where no dominant strategy does: each firm's best choice depends on the rival's move, but once both have chosen, neither can improve alone. Dominant strategy is a sufficient condition for part of a Nash equilibrium; Nash equilibrium is the broader concept that captures all stable strategy pairs.

transferQuestion.questionText: Two firms, X and Y, play a pricing game. Firm X can charge High or Low. Firm Y can charge High or Low. If X plays High and Y plays High, X earns £50m and Y earns £50m. If X plays High and Y plays Low, X earns £20m and Y earns £70m. If X plays Low and Y plays High, X earns £60m and Y earns £30m. If X plays Low and Y plays Low, X earns £40m and Y earns £40m. Does Firm X have a dominant strategy? If so, which strategy is it, and explain why that strategy will definitely appear in any Nash equilibrium of this game.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: No, Firm X does not have a dominant strategy. Explanation must show: when Y plays High, X's best response is Low (£60m > £50m); when Y plays Low, X's best response is High (£40m < £20m is false—£40m > £20m is false; actually £20m < £40m means Low is better, £40m > £20m). Recalculate: if Y plays Low, X earns £20m (High) vs £40m (Low), so Low is better. If Y plays High, X earns £50m (High) vs £60m (Low), so Low is better. [Correction: Low always gives £60m or £40m; High always gives £50m or £20m. Low strictly dominates.] A correct answer identifies that Low is X's dominant strategy and notes that because Low is dominant, it must form part of any Nash equilibrium because X will always choose it and rivals know this.

integrationQuestion.questionText: In a three-firm oligopoly, Firm A discovers that its strategy 'Invest in R&D' is a dominant strategy—it yields higher profit than 'Do not invest' no matter what B and C choose. Firm B has no dominant strategy; its best move depends on C's choice. Explain why the Nash equilibrium of this game must include Firm A investing in R&D, but cannot be determined by examining only Firm B's payoffs in isolation. What additional information would you need to find the full Nash equilibrium?
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must include: (1) Firm A has a dominant strategy (Invest), so it will always choose Invest—this is certain and does not depend on rivals; therefore any Nash equilibrium must have Firm A investing. (2) Firm B's best choice depends on what C does, so Firm B's decision cannot be determined until C's strategy is specified; examining only B's payoffs in isolation reveals no dominant strategy and thus does not pin down B's choice. (3) Additional information needed: either the payoff matrix for Firm C or an assumption about how C will respond to A and B's choices (i.e., C's strategy or payoff structure) to determine B's optimal response and hence the full equilibrium. Award full mark only if all three elements are present and clearly explained.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Nash equilibrium explains why the prisoner's dilemma outcome is self-reinforcing in oligopoly. Each firm's dominant strategy (undercutting) leads to a Nash equilibrium because, once both firms set low prices, neither can improve profit by switching alone—if one raises price while the rival stays low, it loses sales and earns less. The dilemma's tragedy is that this stable Nash outcome yields lower joint profits than cooperation would. Without Nash equilibrium, the prisoner's dilemma would be merely a payoff comparison; Nash equilibrium reveals why rational, independent firms become trapped in it.

transferQuestion.questionText: Two car manufacturers compete on warranty length. Firm A observes that Firm B offers a 3-year warranty. If A switches unilaterally to a 5-year warranty while B stays at 3 years, A's market share falls and its total profit drops from £80m to £60m. Firm B faces the same payoff structure. Currently both offer 3-year warranties and both earn £80m profit. Explain why this 3-year outcome satisfies Nash equilibrium and illustrate why this represents a prisoner's dilemma for the firms.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must identify: (1) neither firm can unilaterally improve profit by switching from 3 years (A would fall to £60m, same for B) = Nash equilibrium condition met; (2) both firms would earn higher profit (>£80m) if they jointly agreed to stay at 3 years rather than escalating to 5 years = joint payoff exists but is not chosen due to incentive to defect. Answers that only define Nash equilibrium or prisoner's dilemma without connecting both concepts to this scenario = incorrect.

integrationQuestion.questionText: Two airlines set fares independently. The payoff matrix shows: if both charge £200, each earns £50m; if one charges £150 while the other charges £200, the low-price firm earns £70m and the high-price firm earns £20m. (a) Identify the Nash equilibrium outcome and explain why it occurs. (b) Why might both airlines have been better off in the £200-£200 scenario, and what does this reveal about the relationship between Nash equilibrium and cooperative outcomes?
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct: (a) Nash equilibrium is both charge £150 (each firm's best response to the rival's choice: if rival charges £150, you earn £50m by matching and lose £20m by staying at £200; if rival charges £200, you earn £70m by undercutting and lose £30m by staying high). Neither can unilaterally improve by switching. (b) At £200-£200, each earned £50m; at £150-£150 they each earn less. This is the prisoner's dilemma: both rationally reach a worse joint outcome because each firm's individual incentive to undercut dominates cooperation. Answers that correctly identify £150 as Nash equilibrium but fail to explain (i) why unilateral deviation doesn't improve profit or (ii) the cooperative-competitive trade-off = partial/incomplete.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Interdependence creates the prisoner's dilemma: because each firm's profit genuinely depends on what its rival does, each must choose a strategy without knowing the rival's choice for certain. This mutual strategic uncertainty is what makes the dilemma possible. If firms were independent (as in perfect competition), each would simply set price equal to marginal cost regardless of rivals, so no dilemma would exist. Interdependence forces each oligopolist to calculate: "If my rival cuts price, should I cut too?" This logic—that undercutting yields higher profit whatever the rival does—leads both to the dominant strategy of low price, trapping them in a mutually worse outcome despite cooperation being jointly profitable.

transferQuestion.questionText: Two cereal manufacturers, Kellogg's and Nestlé, both face a choice: launch an expensive advertising campaign or keep advertising spending low. If both keep spending low, each earns £50m profit. If one advertises heavily and the other doesn't, the advertiser earns £80m and the rival earns £20m. If both advertise heavily, each earns £30m. Explain why this situation represents a prisoner's dilemma in oligopoly, and identify what each firm's dominant strategy is.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer: Each firm's dominant strategy is to advertise heavily (£30m is higher than £20m if rival advertises; £80m is higher than £50m if rival doesn't). This is a prisoner's dilemma because: (1) firms are interdependent—each firm's payoff depends on both its own choice and the rival's choice; (2) the dominant strategy for both (heavy advertising) leads to mutual outcome of £30m, which is worse than the cooperative joint outcome of £50m if both kept spending low; (3) neither firm can escape by unilaterally changing strategy once both advertise, since switching to low spending drops its profit to £20m. Award credit only if all three elements are clearly explained.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A government competition regulator has proposed a rule: "Any oligopolist that undercuts the market price by more than 5% faces a £100m fine." Two rival firms currently earn £40m each under a mutual price-cutting equilibrium. If both firms raise prices (moving away from undercutting), each would earn £65m. Using your understanding of interdependence and the prisoner's dilemma, explain whether this fine rule would be likely to succeed in shifting the firms away from price-cutting, and why.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must address: (1) Interdependence means each firm's profit still depends on the rival's choice even with the fine present; (2) The fine changes the payoff structure for undercutting (now -£60m net, or £40m−£100m), making it no longer the dominant strategy if the rival doesn't undercut; (3) However, the rule succeeds only if both firms believe the other will comply—if either firm suspects the other will risk the fine to earn higher profit, it faces the same dilemma logic (undercut to get ahead or cooperate and trust); (4) The rule removes the prisoner's dilemma trap by raising the cost of defection, but cooperation now requires each firm to trust the other will obey the rule, shifting the problem from economic incentives to credibility of enforcement. Award full credit only if interdependence is referenced and the tension between incentive-change and the persistence of strategic uncertainty is explained.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Collusion only makes sense as a rational choice *because* firms are interdependent. If each firm's actions didn't directly affect rivals' profits, there would be no motive to coordinate with them—a firm could simply maximise its own profit independently. Interdependence creates the strategic dilemma: each firm fears rivals will undercut price or expand output, eroding everyone's profit. Collusion solves this by converting that mutual vulnerability into mutual agreement, turning interdependence from a threat into a mechanism for joint gain. Without interdependence, collusion would be unnecessary; firms would ignore each other entirely.

transferQuestion.questionText: In a market dominated by three large airlines, Carrier A is considering whether to reduce ticket prices on routes where all three operate. Explain why Carrier A would need to predict its rivals' responses before making this decision, and briefly outline how a formal collusive agreement between the three carriers might address the problem this creates.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) identify that price reduction by A will directly reduce B and C's revenue/demand on shared routes (interdependence), (2) note that B and C are likely to respond (e.g. match the price cut, escalate competition), (3) explain that A faces uncertainty about the scale/type of response, (4) state that collusion would reduce this uncertainty by coordinating pricing to mutual benefit, preventing destructive price competition. Accept reference to matching price cuts, price wars, or loss of profit for all three firms. Incorrect: only mentions A's own profit, or treats rivals' reactions as irrelevant.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A proposed merger between two firms in an oligopolistic industry would increase the combined firm's market share from 25% to 40%.
