transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answers: (i) MR = 80 − 6Q; (ii) Q = 13.33 (or 13⅓ units); (iii) P = £40. All three must be correct. Award mark only if all three are correct; otherwise zero.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A monopolist's demand curve is P = 120 − 2Q. The firm's marginal cost is constant at MC = 40. (i) Calculate the revenue-maximising output and the price at that output. (ii) Calculate the profit-maximising output and price. (iii) Explain why the firm would not choose to maximise revenue if its objective is to maximise profit.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answers: (i) Revenue max: MR = 120 − 4Q, so MR = 0 when Q = 30; P = 60. (ii) Profit max: MC = MR, so 40 = 120 − 4Q, Q = 20; P = 80. (iii) At revenue-maximising output (Q = 30), MR = 0 but MC = 40 > 0, so producing the 31st unit adds negative profit (price falls but cost stays the same). Profit-maximising output is where MC = MR = 40, which occurs at lower output (Q = 20) and higher price (P = 80); at this point each additional unit up to Q = 20 adds more to revenue than to cost. Award full mark only if all three parts are correct with reasoning in (iii) that explicitly references MR = 0 implying zero marginal contribution to profit.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: The diagrammatic method for price discrimination only works because the three necessary conditions already hold. Market power allows the firm to set different prices rather than accept one equilibrium price. The ability to identify and separate consumers by group is what creates the two distinct demand curves you draw side by side—without separation, there would be only one combined market. Prevention of leakage ensures each sub-market's demand curve stays independent; if consumers could arbitrage between segments, the two curves would merge and the diagram collapses into a single-market case. The diagram therefore visualises a situation that is only possible when all three conditions are satisfied.

transferQuestion.questionText: A cinema charges £8 to adults and £5 to children for the same film. The child segment has more price-elastic demand than the adult segment. In a two-market diagram for this price discrimination, explain why it would be incorrect to draw the two demand curves at identical positions (i.e. overlapping exactly), and what condition must hold to justify drawing them separately.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must state: (1) Identical demand curves would imply identical price elasticities, but the problem specifies children's demand is more elastic than adults', so the curves must differ in slope/position, OR that different elasticities require different demand curves; AND (2) The cinema must be able to prevent arbitrage/seepage (children or adults reselling tickets to the other group) for the two markets to remain separate—this is the third condition preventing leakage. Accept equivalent reasoning. Incorrect: answers that merely restate the profit rule or do not address elasticity differences or prevention of resale.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A firm practising third-degree price discrimination across two markets discovers that after drawing its two-market diagram and finding the profit-maximising output in each segment using the common MC rule, it observes that Price₁ = £10 and Price₂ = £6, with MR₁ = MR₂ = £3 (the common MC). One month later, consumers in Market 2 gain access to an online resale platform and begin buying at £6 and reselling to Market 1 consumers at £8, undercutting the £10 price. Explain why this development would invalidate the diagrammatic solution and which of the three necessary conditions has been violated.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) Explain that the two demand curves no longer remain independent because arbitrage/resale creates a single effective price (around £8), so the separate demand curves in the diagram no longer represent the firm's actual choice set, making the side-by-side diagram analysis obsolete; AND (2) Identify that the third necessary condition—prevention of leakage/arbitrage between markets—has been violated. The firm no longer satisfies all three conditions, so price discrimination breaks down. Accept: 'market segmentation fails' or 'resale prevents separation'. Incorrect: answers that do not link the resale activity to a breakdown in the diagrammatic method, or that misidentify which condition is violated.

edgeLessons.linkTeaching: Government policy and infrastructure raise competitiveness by lowering production costs and improving efficiency. Unit labour costs capture one crucial dimension of this: if infrastructure reduces bottlenecks and policy encourages worker training, productivity rises faster than wages, pushing unit labour costs down. Conversely, poor infrastructure and weak skills policy keep productivity flat while wages rise, pushing unit labour costs up relative to competitors. RULCs therefore embody the supply-side effects of policy and infrastructure in a measurable price-competitiveness metric—they show whether government's choices have successfully positioned a country to compete on cost.

transferQuestion.questionText: Country X invests heavily in port and rail infrastructure, reducing cargo handling time by 40%. Simultaneously, it raises the minimum wage by 8%. Over two years, output per worker increases by 12%. Explain what happens to Country X's relative unit labour costs compared to trading partners whose policy and infrastructure remain unchanged, and why.
transferQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must state: (1) RULCs fall/improve (or index number falls relative to trading partners); (2) reasoning must identify that productivity growth (12%) exceeds wage growth (8%), so unit labour cost per output falls domestically; (3) must attribute this productivity gain to infrastructure investment (port/rail efficiency), showing that improved infrastructure drives the competitiveness benefit into the RULC measure. Accept alternative phrasing of the mechanism. Do not accept answers that only mention wage rises or only mention infrastructure without connecting both to the productivity-versus-wage gap.

integrationQuestion.questionText: A government cuts corporation tax but simultaneously reduces spending on vocational training. In the same period, the country's RULC index rises relative to its main trading partner. Using concepts of policy, infrastructure, and unit labour costs, explain one way this outcome is possible and why it suggests the policy package was poorly targeted for competitiveness.
integrationQuestion.markScheme: Correct answer must: (1) identify that reduced training spending weakens human capital/labour productivity growth; (2) explain that without strong productivity growth, wages (perhaps rising due to skills shortage or tight labour market) grow faster than output per worker, raising unit labour cost; (3) conclude that lower corporation tax alone does not offset the RULC deterioration because it does not drive the productivity gains needed to outpace wage growth; (4) state or imply that the government neglected the supply-side factor (training/infrastructure development) that actually translates policy into lower relative unit labour costs. Accept reasoning that focuses on skills/training; accept reasoning centred on any infrastructure omission. Do not accept answers that invoke only tax cuts or only wage/price effects without linking to productivity.
